Naive Bayes

Naive Bayes is a classifier that uses Bayes' theorem to score each class as its prior probability multiplied by the probability of every observed feature given that class, and predicts the class with the highest score. It is called naive because it treats the features as independent of one another once the class is known.

1Overview

Why it matters

Naive Bayes is the classifier to try first when the input is text, or any long list of individually weak clues, and labelled data is scarce: is this email spam, which queue should this ticket go to, what language is this page written in. Training is one pass of counting, prediction is a few table look-ups and additions, and the model can be updated one example at a time. That makes it a standard baseline, and it is still a working part of mail filters, language detectors and scientific pipelines, as the examples below show.

What goes wrong is rarely the algorithm. A word that was never seen with a class gets probability zero and vetoes that class because nobody turned on smoothing. The wrong variant is used, such as Gaussian densities on word counts. Or the output of predict_proba is read as a trustworthy probability when correlated features have pushed it towards 0 or 1. Anyone who builds or reviews a text classifier, or who puts a threshold on a model's score, needs to recognise these three failures.

Before you start

  • Probability for MLBeginner

What you will be able to do

  • Derive the naive Bayes decision rule from Bayes' theorem and state what the conditional independence assumption claims.
  • Compute priors, smoothed word likelihoods and the posterior for a short message by hand, and match scikit-learn's output.
  • Choose between the Gaussian, multinomial and Bernoulli variants from the type of the features.
  • Explain the zero-frequency problem and how additive (Laplace or Lidstone) smoothing fixes it.
  • Explain why naive Bayes probabilities are overconfident and say when that matters.

Key terms

Prior
The probability of a class before looking at any features, usually estimated as the share of training examples that belong to it.
Likelihood
The probability of seeing a particular feature value among examples of one class, written P(x | y).
Posterior
The probability of a class after the features have been taken into account, written P(y | x). The classifier compares it across classes.
Conditional independence
The assumption that once the class is known, learning the value of one feature tells you nothing more about any other feature.
Bag of words
A representation of a text as the count of each word it contains, with word order thrown away.
Vocabulary
The set of distinct words, or other tokens, seen in the training data. Each one becomes a feature.
Additive smoothing
Adding a small constant, alpha, to every count before converting counts to probabilities, so that nothing unseen gets probability zero. Alpha of 1 is Laplace smoothing and a smaller value is Lidstone smoothing.
Log-likelihood
The logarithm of a likelihood. Adding logs replaces multiplying many small probabilities, which would round down to zero.
MAP class
The maximum a posteriori class, meaning the class with the highest posterior probability. It is the classifier's prediction.
Calibration
How well predicted probabilities match observed frequencies. Predictions of 0.8 from a calibrated model are right about 80 percent of the time.

2Explanation

Introduction

You already sort mail this way. A message that says "win", "prize" and "claim now" is probably junk, and one that mentions "meeting" and "notes" is probably from a colleague. No single word settles it. Each word is a clue that makes one class more or less likely, and you weigh the clues together.

Naive Bayes does the weighing with Bayes' theorem, the rule for updating a probability when evidence arrives. For a class yyy (spam, or ham, the usual name for legitimate mail) and a message xxx:

P(y∣x)=P(y) P(x∣y)P(x)P(y \mid x) = \frac{P(y)\,P(x \mid y)}{P(x)}P(y∣x)=P(x)P(y)P(x∣y)​

P(y)P(y)P(y) is the prior: how common the class is before anything has been read. P(x∣y)P(x \mid y)P(x∣y) is the likelihood: how probable this message is among messages of that class. P(y∣x)P(y \mid x)P(y∣x) is the posterior, the number we want.

The likelihood is the hard part. A whole message has almost certainly never appeared in the training data, so its probability cannot be counted directly. The naive step is to pretend that, within a class, each word turns up independently of the others. The probability of the message is then the product of the probabilities of its words, and a word's probability can be counted: how often does "cash" occur in spam, and how often in ham?

Training is therefore counting. Prediction is looking up the counts for the words of a new message, combining them with the prior, and picking the class with the larger result. With the eight training messages used later in this lesson, "free cash now" comes out as spam by 0.89 to 0.11.

The assumption is false for real text, where "hong" is rarely far from "kong", and the method often classifies well anyway. This lesson explains why. It covers the three standard variants (multinomial for counts, Bernoulli for yes/no features, Gaussian for measurements), the smoothing that stops an unseen word from vetoing a class, and one text classification example worked by hand and in scikit-learn. Text classification is the classic use, so it is the running example.

How it works

From Bayes' theorem to a decision rule

Write an input as features x1,…,xnx_1, \dots, x_nx1​,…,xn​; for text, the words. Bayes' theorem gives the posterior of each class yyy:

P(y∣x1,…,xn)=P(y) P(x1,…,xn∣y)P(x1,…,xn)P(y \mid x_1, \dots, x_n) = \frac{P(y)\,P(x_1, \dots, x_n \mid y)}{P(x_1, \dots, x_n)}P(y∣x1​,…,xn​)=P(x1​,…,xn​)P(y)P(x1​,…,xn​∣y)​

The denominator is the same for every class, so it cannot change which class wins. Only the numerators need comparing.

The joint likelihood P(x1,…,xn∣y)P(x_1, \dots, x_n \mid y)P(x1​,…,xn​∣y) is the obstacle. With a vocabulary of MMM words, a table with an entry for every combination of present and absent words needs about 2M2^M2M numbers per class, as Introduction to Information Retrieval (the IR book (opens in a new tab) from here on) points out. The conditional independence assumption replaces it with a product of one-feature terms:

P(x1,…,xn∣y)=∏i=1nP(xi∣y)P(x_1, \dots, x_n \mid y) = \prod_{i=1}^{n} P(x_i \mid y)P(x1​,…,xn​∣y)=i=1∏n​P(xi​∣y)

In words: once the class is known, learning one feature's value tells you nothing more about the others. Now about MMM numbers per class are enough, and each is a simple frequency. The prediction is the MAP class, the one with the highest posterior:

y^=arg⁡max⁡y[log⁡P(y)+∑i=1nlog⁡P(xi∣y)]\hat{y} = \arg\max_y \Big[ \log P(y) + \sum_{i=1}^{n} \log P(x_i \mid y) \Big]y^​=argymax​[logP(y)+i=1∑n​logP(xi​∣y)]

Logs are used because a product of many small probabilities underflows. In double precision, 300 factors of 0.05 multiply to exactly 0.0, while their logs add up to −898.7. Taking logs does not change which class is largest. To get probabilities back, exponentiate the scores and divide each by their sum.

Three variants, three models of one feature

The variants differ only in how they model P(xi∣y)P(x_i \mid y)P(xi​∣y).

Multinomial is for counts, typically word counts. Each class has one probability per word, estimated from all the text of that class:

θ^yi=Nyi+αNy+αn\hat{\theta}_{yi} = \frac{N_{yi} + \alpha}{N_y + \alpha n}θ^yi​=Ny​+αnNyi​+α​

NyiN_{yi}Nyi​ is the number of times word iii occurs in class yyy, NyN_yNy​ is the class's total word count, nnn is the vocabulary size and α\alphaα is the smoothing constant explained below. A word that occurs three times in a document contributes its log-probability three times.

Bernoulli is for yes/no features: does the word occur in the document at all? Each class has a probability pyip_{yi}pyi​ that one of its documents contains word iii, estimated as (documents of the class that contain it + α+\,\alpha+α) divided by (documents of the class + 2α+\,2\alpha+2α). The likelihood of one feature is

P(xi∣y)=pyi xi+(1−pyi)(1−xi)P(x_i \mid y) = p_{yi}\,x_i + (1 - p_{yi})(1 - x_i)P(xi​∣y)=pyi​xi​+(1−pyi​)(1−xi​)

so an absent word also contributes, through 1−pyi1 - p_{yi}1−pyi​. The multinomial model ignores absent words. The IR book warns (opens in a new tab) that the Bernoulli model makes many mistakes on long documents, where one occurrence counts as much as fifty.

Gaussian is for continuous measurements. Each class stores a mean μyi\mu_{yi}μyi​ and a variance σyi2\sigma^2_{yi}σyi2​ for each feature, and the likelihood is the height of the normal curve:

P(xi∣y)=12πσyi2exp⁡(−(xi−μyi)22σyi2)P(x_i \mid y) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi\sigma^2_{yi}}} \exp\left(-\frac{(x_i - \mu_{yi})^2}{2\sigma^2_{yi}}\right)P(xi​∣y)=2πσyi2​​1​exp(−2σyi2​(xi​−μyi​)2​)

Take one feature, the vibration of a machine bearing in mm/s, with illustrative numbers: healthy bearings average 2.0 with a standard deviation of 0.4, and worn ones average 3.0 with 0.6. A reading of 2.4 has density 0.605 under "healthy" and 0.403 under "worn". With equal priors the posterior for healthy is 0.605/(0.605+0.403)=0.600.605 / (0.605 + 0.403) = 0.600.605/(0.605+0.403)=0.60. If 90 % of bearings are healthy it becomes 0.9×0.605/(0.9×0.605+0.1×0.403)=0.930.9 \times 0.605 / (0.9 \times 0.605 + 0.1 \times 0.403) = 0.930.9×0.605/(0.9×0.605+0.1×0.403)=0.93.

scikit-learn (opens in a new tab) ships two more variants built on the same idea:

Smoothing

Without smoothing (α=0\alpha = 0α=0), a word that never occurred with a class has likelihood 0, and one zero makes the whole product zero whatever the other words say. This is the zero-frequency problem. Additive smoothing pretends every word was seen α\alphaα extra times in every class. α=1\alpha = 1α=1 is Laplace (add-one) smoothing and 0<α<10 < \alpha < 10<α<1 is Lidstone smoothing. A large α\alphaα flattens every likelihood towards uniform, so the prior takes over; a tiny α\alphaα lets one rare word swing the result. Treat α\alphaα as a hyperparameter and choose it by cross-validation.

Smoothing covers words in the vocabulary that one class has not seen. A word that appears in no training document is not in the vocabulary, and it is dropped at prediction time.

GaussianNB has a different safeguard. Its var_smoothing (opens in a new tab) parameter (default 1e-9) adds that fraction of the largest feature variance to every variance, so a feature that is constant within a class does not cause a division by zero.

Text classification in practice

The standard pipeline turns each document into a bag of words, a vector of word counts that ignores order, and gives it to the multinomial model:

python
from sklearn.feature_extraction.text import CountVectorizer
from sklearn.naive_bayes import MultinomialNB
from sklearn.pipeline import make_pipeline

model = make_pipeline(CountVectorizer(), MultinomialNB(alpha=1.0))
model.fit(train_texts, train_labels)       # lists of strings
model.predict(["free cash now"])

By default CountVectorizer (opens in a new tab) lowercases the text, treats punctuation as a separator and keeps tokens of two or more characters. MultinomialNB (opens in a new tab) expects counts, though its documentation notes that fractional weights such as tf-idf may also work. Because training is only counting, partial_fit can update the model batch by batch when the data does not fit in memory.

Why a wrong assumption still classifies well

Words in real text are not independent. When features are correlated, naive Bayes counts the same evidence more than once, which pushes the winning class's probability towards 1 and the rest towards 0. The ranking of the classes usually survives, so accuracy holds up. The IR book's summary is that naive Bayes classifiers estimate badly but often classify well, and scikit-learn's guide says the outputs of predict_proba are not to be taken too seriously. If you need a probability to set a threshold or attach a cost, calibrate the model first (see scikit-learn's calibration guide (opens in a new tab)) and judge it with the classification metrics that match your costs.

Worked example: Classifying two short messages as spam or ham, by hand and with scikit-learn

Eight training messages, invented so that the arithmetic stays tidy. Three are spam and five are ham.

#MessageClass

In log space the same scores are −0.981+3×(−1.897)=−6.672-0.981 + 3 \times (-1.897) = -6.672−0.981+3×(−1.897)=−6.672 for spam and −0.470−2.526−3.219−2.526≈−8.740-0.470 - 2.526 - 3.219 - 2.526 \approx -8.740−0.470−2.526−3.219−2.526≈−8.740 for ham. "about" is not in the vocabulary, so it is dropped. Three words remain.

Step 5: the same messages without smoothing

With α=0\alpha = 0α=0, P(cash∣ham)=0/15=0P(\text{cash} \mid \text{ham}) = 0/15 = 0P(cash∣ham)=0/15=0 and P(meeting∣spam)=P(today∣spam)=0/10=0P(\text{meeting} \mid \text{spam}) = P(\text{today} \mid \text{spam}) = 0/10 = 0P(meeting∣spam)=P(today∣spam)=0/10=0.

  • "free cash now": the ham score is 0.625×115×0×115=00.625 \times \tfrac{1}{15} \times 0 \times \tfrac{1}{15} = 00.625×151​×0×151​=0, so P(spam)=1P(\text{spam}) = 1P(spam)=1 exactly. Total certainty from eight messages is not believable.
  • "meeting today about cash": the spam score contains two zeros and the ham score one. Both scores are 0 and the posterior is 0/00/00/0. scikit-learn returns nan for both classes.

Step 6: check with scikit-learn

python
import numpy as np
from sklearn.feature_extraction.text import CountVectorizer
from sklearn.naive_bayes import MultinomialNB

messages = [
    "win cash now", "free cash prize", "win free prize now",
    "project meeting today", "lunch meeting today", "free lunch today",
    "project notes now", "meeting notes today",
]
labels = ["spam"] * 3 + ["ham"] * 5

vectorizer = CountVectorizer()
X = vectorizer.fit_transform(messages)       # one row per message, one column per word
model = MultinomialNB(alpha=1.0).fit(X, labels)
print("classes:", model.classes_, "priors:", np.exp(model.class_log_prior_))

tests = ["free cash now", "meeting today about cash"]
X_new = vectorizer.transform(tests)          # "about" is not in the vocabulary and is dropped
for text, label, proba in zip(tests, model.predict(X_new), model.predict_proba(X_new)):
    print(f"{text!r}: {label}  P(ham) = {proba[0]:.4f}  P(spam) = {proba[1]:.4f}")

Output with scikit-learn 1.9.1:

text
classes: ['ham' 'spam'] priors: [0.625 0.375]
'free cash now': spam  P(ham) = 0.1122  P(spam) = 0.8878
'meeting today about cash': ham  P(ham) = 0.8505  P(spam) = 0.1495

np.exp(model.feature_log_prob_) reproduces the two likelihood columns of the table.

BernoulliNB(alpha=1.0) on the same matrix gives P(spam)=0.972P(\text{spam}) = 0.972P(spam)=0.972 for "free cash now", not 0.888. It estimates, for each word, the share of a class's messages that contain it, and then also multiplies in the absent words. The first bracket holds the three words that are present, and the rest are the seven absent ones.

What the result means

Both variants agree on the labels and disagree on how sure to be, and neither probability deserves trust on eight training messages. What the example does establish is the mechanism: the prior sets a starting point, each word multiplies the score by its likelihood, and smoothing keeps any single word from having the final say.

Edge cases and limitations

A word never seen with a class gives that class a probability of zero
With alpha set to 0, one zero likelihood wipes out all other evidence for the class. In the worked example "meeting today about cash" then scores 0 for both classes and scikit-learn returns nan. The zero means the word has not been seen with the class yet, which is weaker than impossible. Keep alpha above 0 and tune it by cross-validation, starting from a grid such as 0.01, 0.1, 0.5 and 1.
Repeated or redundant evidence is counted every time it appears
Each copy of a correlated feature multiplies the score again. In the worked example "free cash now" has a spam probability of 0.888; writing "cash" twice raises it to 0.967 and three times to 0.991, although the repeats add no information. A duplicated sensor column does the same to GaussianNB (exercise 2 has a case where it flips the prediction). Remove near-duplicate features, cap repeated tokens with binary counts, and do not read the resulting probabilities as confidence.
The Bernoulli model on long documents
Bernoulli features record only whether a word occurs, so one stray mention in a 50-page report weighs as much as a word used on every page. The IR book's example is a whole book assigned to the class China because the term occurs in it once. Use the multinomial model when document length varies a lot, and keep Bernoulli for short texts such as subject lines or search queries.
GaussianNB on features that are not bell-shaped within a class
A normal curve is a poor model for counts that are mostly zero, for heavily skewed amounts and for features with two clusters inside one class. The fitted mean and variance then describe values that rarely occur, and the likelihoods mislead. Plot a histogram of each feature per class first. Log-transform skewed positive features, or cut them into bins and use CategoricalNB.
var_smoothing can erase a feature measured on a tiny scale
GaussianNB adds 1e-9 times the largest feature variance to every variance. Re-express the exercise 2 data with the temperature in thousandths of a degree (multiply by 1000, so its variance is in the millions) and the vibration in inches per second (divide mm/s by 25.4, so its class variances are about 0.0001 and 0.0002). The amount added is then 0.022, about a hundred times the vibration variances or more. By our calculation the probability of healthy for the new reading moves from 0.527 to 0.711, almost exactly what temperature alone gives (0.710). Standardise features before GaussianNB when their scales differ by many orders of magnitude.
Word order and negation are invisible to a bag of words
"not good, bad" and "not bad, good" contain the same words and therefore get the same score. Naive Bayes cannot learn that "not" reverses the word after it, because every feature contributes independently of its neighbours. Adding two-word features (ngram_range=(1, 2) in CountVectorizer) recovers some of this at the cost of a larger vocabulary and more correlated features.

When to use it, and when something simpler is enough

Use it when

  • The input is text, or another long list of sparse and individually weak features, and you want a working baseline within minutes.
  • Labelled data is small, from tens to a few thousand examples per class, where a model with one number per feature and class is hard to overfit.
  • The model has to learn continuously from a stream of corrections, as a mail filter does, or from data too large for memory, using partial_fit.
  • Prediction must be very cheap, a few look-ups and additions per feature, and the model must be small enough to ship as a table.
  • There are hundreds or thousands of classes, some with only a handful of examples, and each class can be estimated from its own counts.

Think twice when

  • You need probabilities you can act on, for example to set a threshold from a cost ratio. Use logistic regression, or calibrate the naive Bayes output first.
  • The signal lies in combinations of features, such as word order, negation or the ratio of two measurements. Naive Bayes cannot represent an interaction.
  • Many features measure nearly the same thing and you cannot prune them. The duplicated evidence will dominate the score.
  • Accuracy is the priority and you have enough labelled data for a discriminative model such as logistic regression or gradient boosting. Keep naive Bayes as the baseline they must beat.

A simpler alternative. Predict the most common class for everything, or write a keyword rule. The majority class is what naive Bayes itself falls back to when a message contains no known words, so it is the honest floor to compare against. A keyword list stops being enough when no single word is decisive and the evidence from many words has to be weighed, which is what the per-word likelihoods do.

Key takeaways

  • Naive Bayes scores each class as its prior times the likelihood of every feature, assuming the features are independent given the class, and predicts the class with the highest score.
  • Training is counting and prediction is adding log-probabilities, so the method is fast, can learn incrementally and works on small data.
  • The variant follows the feature type. Use multinomial for counts, Bernoulli for present-or-absent features and Gaussian for continuous measurements.
  • Always smooth. Without an added constant, one word that was never seen with a class gives that class a probability of exactly zero.
  • The independence assumption counts correlated evidence more than once, so the predicted class is often right while the predicted probability is too extreme to use without calibration.

3Real-world applications

5 documented uses of Naive Bayes. Each one names the real system, the problem it solves and its tradeoff, with links to the sources.

  1. Apache SpamAssassin: a Bayesian mail classifier trained on each site's own mail
  2. CLD2 at Common Crawl: naming the language of billions of web pages
  3. RDP Classifier and QIIME 2: assigning bacterial gene sequences to taxa
  4. NOAA Enterprise Cloud Mask: a naive Bayesian cloud detector for satellite imagers
  5. GnuCash: suggesting the account for an imported bank transaction

Example 1 of 5

Apache SpamAssassin: a Bayesian mail classifier trained on each site's own mail

Apache SpamAssassinDocumented in official docs

Apache SpamAssassin is an open-source mail filter. Its sa-learn manual and its configuration reference describe a built-in "naive-Bayesian-style" classifier that is trained on the site's own mail. For how the method works, the manual points to Paul Graham's 2002 essay "A Plan for Spam", in which Graham describes the filter in the web-based mail reader that he and his colleagues built. [11][12][13]

The problem

Hand-written rules catch spam by known phrases and header tricks, but spammers change their wording, and what counts as spam differs from one mailbox to the next. The sa-learn manual lists what a learned classifier adds: it can greatly reduce false positives and false negatives, and it is tailored to the site's mail flow because it learns from that mail. Graham's essay sets the priority: for most users, losing a legitimate message is far worse than receiving a spam, so false positives matter most.

Where this topic fits

The classifier is one component among SpamAssassin's rules. Mail that an administrator or user has sorted into spam and ham is fed to sa-learn, which updates a database of tokens and how often each has been seen in each kind of mail. When a new message is scanned, its tokens are looked up and combined into a spam probability, which is reported through the BAYES rules beside the hand-written ones. Messages that the whole rule set scores very high or very low can be fed back into training automatically.

How it is applied, step by step

  1. Collect hand-sorted mail from the site itself, one folder of spam and one of ham. Both are required: the manual says training on one type alone has no effect.
  2. Run sa-learn --spam and sa-learn --ham on the folders. Each message is split into tokens, by default taken from headers, visible and invisible text and URIs, and the spam and ham counts stored for those tokens are increased.
  3. The Bayes rules stay inactive until enough mail has been learned, by default 200 spam and 200 ham messages, because estimates from a handful of messages are unreliable.
  4. For an incoming message, look up each token and turn its two counts into a probability that a message containing it is spam. In Graham's version a token never seen before is given 0.4.
  5. Combine the per-token probabilities into one score. Graham multiplies the probabilities of the fifteen tokens furthest from 0.5 and normalises, which is the naive Bayes product with equal priors.
  6. Feed corrections back. Re-running sa-learn with the right label undoes a wrong one, and auto-learning adds confidently scored mail without manual sorting.

Why this approach fits

The training data arrives as a stream: every message a user files as junk or rescues from the junk folder is a new labelled example, and naive Bayes absorbs it by incrementing a few counts, with no retraining run. The features are thousands of tokens, each weak alone, which is the setting where adding up independent evidence works. Because the counts come from one site's mail, the model encodes that site's vocabulary: a word that marks spam for one organisation is ordinary business for another. Graham adds a security argument, that per-user word probabilities make it hard for a spammer to tune one message against everybody's filter.

Limitation or tradeoff

The classifier needs a decent amount of correctly sorted mail before it helps, and the manual warns that without regular retraining its data goes stale. Verdicts are hard to explain to a user, since there is no single matched rule to point at. The token database costs disk space and memory. Mislabelled training mail, or folders that contain forwarded spam and discussions about spam, teach it the wrong associations. The independence assumption also shows: Graham notes that few messages end up with a probability in the middle of the range, so his 0.9 threshold could sit almost anywhere.

What the sources document

  • The configuration reference describes use_bayes (default 1) as the switch for "the naive-Bayesian-style classifier built into SpamAssassin", and says the Bayes system does not activate until 200 ham and 200 spam messages have been learned by default (bayes_min_ham_num and bayes_min_spam_num). [12]
  • bayes_auto_learn (default 1) controls whether SpamAssassin automatically feeds high-scoring mails, or low-scoring mails for non-spam, into its learning system. [12]
  • The sa-learn manual says training needs both spam and ham, suggests aiming for at least 1,000 messages of each, reports that more than about 5,000 did not improve accuracy significantly in the project's tests, and urges training on mail from your own server and not a public corpus. [11]
  • The same manual lists as drawbacks that a decent number of messages is required before results are useful, that it is hard to explain why a message is or is not marked as spam, and that the databases take disk space and memory. [11]
  • Graham describes two corpora of about 4,000 messages each, a per-token spam probability computed from the token counts, a combination of the fifteen most interesting tokens, a spam threshold of 0.9, and a result on his own mail of fewer than 5 missed spams per 1,000 with no false positives. [13]

The facts above come from the cited sources. The steps and analysis in this example are our explanation of how they fit together.

Example 2 of 5

CLD2 at Common Crawl: naming the language of billions of web pages

Common CrawlDocumented in an open-source project

Compact Language Detector 2 (CLD2) is an open-source library whose README, signed by Dick Sites, describes it as a naive Bayesian classifier over letter sequences. Common Crawl, which publishes a free archive of crawled web pages, announced in August 2018 that it runs CLD2 on the HTML pages it crawls and stores the detected languages in its index. [14][15]

The problem

A web crawl contains pages in more than a hundred languages, and the people who use it to build language-specific corpora or indexes need to select pages by language without downloading them. The language a page declares is often missing or wrong, which is why the CLD2 README treats lang tags, the top-level domain and the encoding only as hints. The detector has to run on billions of pages, so it must be extremely fast, and it must cope with pages that mix languages.

Where this topic fits

Language identification is classification with many classes (the README lists 83 languages, and Common Crawl's post says CLD2 can identify 160) and very cheap features: short letter sequences. CLD2 runs in the crawler's processing step, after a page has been fetched and before its index record is written. Its output, up to three languages with scores, is stored with the page.

How it is applied, step by step

  1. Reduce the page to text: expand HTML entities, delete tags, digits and punctuation, and lowercase the remaining letters and marks.
  2. Choose the token type by script. A script used by a single detected language, such as Greek or Thai, decides the answer alone. Han and other CJK text is scored one character at a time. Every other script is scored in sequences of four letters, with word beginnings and endings marked.
  3. Look each sequence up in a precomputed table that holds a few likely languages for it and a quantised log probability for each. The table is the trained model: per-language likelihoods estimated in advance from a large collection of pages.
  4. Add the log probabilities per language across the text. Adding per-sequence log likelihoods is the naive Bayes sum, with each letter sequence treated as independent evidence.
  5. Report the top languages and the share of the text attributed to each. Common Crawl keeps up to three per page and writes their ISO-639-3 codes into its URL index.

Why this approach fits

Letter sequences are cheap and telling: a handful of four-letter fragments narrows the language sharply, and a page supplies hundreds of them, so adding up weak evidence works well. The trained model is a lookup table, which makes prediction a table read and an addition per sequence. That is what allows the speed the README reports, roughly a millisecond for an average page, and what makes a crawl of billions of pages affordable. In a naive Bayes model, training amounts to counting how often each sequence occurs in each language's text, so each language's statistics can be gathered separately.

Limitation or tradeoff

Summed evidence needs enough text. The README sets the design target at pages of at least 200 characters and says CLD2 is not designed for very short text, lists of proper names or part numbers. Closely related languages share most of their letter sequences, so the README describes extra scoring of distinctive words for groups such as Malay and Indonesian. Repetition breaks the independence assumption in a visible way: the README says repeated sequences, such as "jpg" in a list of file names, would skew the score and are removed first, together with words that appear on web pages in every language.

What the sources document

  • The README states that CLD2 is a naive Bayesian classifier using one of three token algorithms: the script alone for scripts that map one-to-one to a detected language, single letters for the Han script and its CJK combinations, and sequences of four letters (quadgrams) for all other scripts. [14]
  • Scoring is done on lowercased Unicode letters and marks after deleting digits, punctuation and tags, and for each letter sequence it uses the 3 to 6 most likely languages and their quantised log probabilities. [14]
  • The README says the training corpus was built from manually chosen web pages for each language and augmented by automated scraping of over 100 million further pages, that the main quadgram table has 256K four-byte entries covering about 50 languages, and that detection on an average 30 KB web page takes roughly 1 millisecond. [14]
  • The stated design target is web pages of at least 200 characters. The README says CLD2 is not designed to do well on very short text, and that repetitive sequences and web-specific words are removed because they would otherwise skew the scoring or carry almost no language information. [14]
  • Common Crawl's August 2018 announcement says it now runs CLD2 on HTML pages to identify the language of a document, with up to three languages per document shown as ISO-639-3 codes in the URL index, and that the crawl contains 2.65 billion web pages. [15]

The facts above come from the cited sources. The steps and analysis in this example are our explanation of how they fit together.

Example 3 of 5

RDP Classifier and QIIME 2: assigning bacterial gene sequences to taxa

RDP Classifier and QIIME 2Documented in a paper

Microbiome studies sequence the 16S rRNA gene of the bacteria in a sample and then need to name the organisms. The RDP Classifier is a naive Bayesian classifier built for this task, described by Wang, Garrity, Tiedje and Cole in a 2007 paper and in an earlier 2004 conference poster. The QIIME 2 analysis platform documents and implements a naive Bayes classifier for the same job in its q2-feature-classifier plugin, which Bokulich and colleagues evaluated in 2018. [16][17][18][20][19]

The problem

A sequencing run yields a large number of short DNA reads, and each must be placed in the bacterial taxonomy: phylum, class, order, family, genus. Reads are often partial, and the classes are numerous and thinly covered: the poster's training set holds about 4,400 type-strain sequences in about 900 genera, roughly five per genus. Some reads come from organisms with no close reference at all, so the method must also report how sure it is. The authors present the classifier as fast, as not requiring sequence alignment and as working well with partial sequences.

Where this topic fits

Classification follows sequence clean-up and comes before any ecological analysis. Each reference sequence of known taxonomy is a training document, and its "words" are overlapping subsequences of fixed length: 8 bases in the RDP Classifier and 7-character sequences in QIIME 2's default pipeline. A read is classified by scoring its words against every genus, and a confidence estimate decides how far down the taxonomy the label may go.

How it is applied, step by step

  1. Cut every reference sequence into overlapping words of 8 bases and record how often each word occurs among the training sequences of each genus. The authors also calculate a word-specific prior from each word's frequency in the entire training set.
  2. Turn the counts into per-genus word probabilities. Because a genus has only a handful of reference sequences, the estimates must be smoothed so that a word missing from one genus does not zero its score. QIIME 2 does this with a small additive constant, alpha = 0.001.
  3. For a query read, multiply the probabilities of its words for each genus, in practice by adding logs. Only words that occur in the query contribute to the score, as in text classifiers. In QIIME 2's default setup no class prior is learned (fit_prior is False), so every taxon starts equal.
  4. Assign the genus with the highest score, then estimate confidence by bootstrap. In each of 100 trials a random one-eighth of the read's words is scored, and the share of trials that pick a genus is its confidence. For higher ranks the results of all genera under a taxon are summed.
  5. Report the assignment only down to the rank that clears a confidence threshold. QIIME 2's classify-sklearn also limits the depth of the label with a default threshold of 0.7, but it takes its confidence from the classifier's predict_proba output, summed over all classes under each taxon, and not from a bootstrap.
  6. In QIIME 2, fit-classifier-naive-bayes trains the classifier on reference reads and their taxonomy. The default pipeline hashes 7-character sequences into 8,192 features and fits a memory-saving variant of scikit-learn's multinomial naive Bayes model.

Why this approach fits

The problem has the shape of text classification: a long string, a vocabulary of short tokens (there are 4^8 = 65,536 possible 8-base words) and classes that differ in which tokens they tend to contain. Counting words needs no alignment, which keeps training and classification fast, and a partial read still supplies plenty of words. With on the order of a thousand classes and very few reference sequences for many of them, a model that estimates each word's frequency separately for each genus is a natural fit, because every estimate needs only that genus's own sequences.

Limitation or tradeoff

Overlapping words are far from independent, since neighbouring 8-base words share seven of their eight bases. The authors say so and score only one-eighth of the words in each bootstrap trial for that reason; our reading is that a confidence taken straight from the raw posterior would be overstated, which is why RDP estimates it by resampling. Accuracy drops for short reads and at fine ranks: in the poster's leave-one-out test genus-level accuracy was 91.0% for near-full-length sequences, 87.7% for 400-base fragments and 46.5% for 200-base fragments, and Bokulich and colleagues found species-level results much less accurate and more variable than higher ranks. A read from an organism missing from the reference set can only be given the name of something that is present, so the confidence threshold is the only protection. Equal class priors ignore that some genera are far more common in a given habitat, which is why Bokulich and colleagues also tested class weights set from the expected composition of the samples.

What the sources document

  • The 2007 abstract describes the RDP Classifier as a naive Bayesian classifier that can rapidly and accurately classify bacterial 16S rRNA sequences, with a confidence estimate for each assignment from domain to genus. It reports overall accuracies of 89% or above down to the genus level for near-full-length and 400-base segments in leave-one-out tests on a corpus of 5,014 type strain sequences and a second corpus of 23,095 sequences. [16]
  • The authors' 2004 poster says the classifier uses all possible eight-base subsequences of the query as its features, calculates word-specific priors from word frequency in the entire training set, lets only the words present in the query contribute to the score as text classifiers do, and is fast, needs no sequence alignment and works well with partial sequences. [17]
  • The poster estimates confidence from 100 bootstrap trials in which a random one-eighth of the query's words is used, because overlapping words are highly dependent, counts how often a genus is selected, and sums the results of the genera under each taxon for higher ranks. Its training set is about 4,400 type-strain sequences in 900 genera. [17]
  • QIIME 2's documentation describes fit-classifier-naive-bayes as creating a scikit-learn naive_bayes classifier for reads, with defaults of an n-gram range of [7, 7], alpha 0.001 and fit_prior False, and gives classify-sklearn a default confidence of 0.7. The plugin's source defines the pipeline as a HashingVectorizer over character 7-grams with 8,192 features followed by a LowMemoryMultinomialNB, and computes confidence from predict_proba. [18][20]
  • Bokulich et al. describe the plugin's classifier as the scikit-learn multinomial naive Bayes classifier and report that species affiliation was predicted with much lower and more variable accuracy among method configurations (median F-measure from 0.42 for UCLUST to 0.95 for naive Bayes with bespoke class weights). They define class weights as the frequency at which each class is expected to be observed. [19]

Example 4 of 5

NOAA Enterprise Cloud Mask: a naive Bayesian cloud detector for satellite imagers

NOAA NESDISDocumented in official docs

The NOAA Enterprise Cloud Mask (ECM) decides, for every pixel of a weather satellite image, whether the view is clear or cloudy. Its Algorithm Theoretical Basis Document (version 1.2, October 2020) describes it as a naive Bayesian approach trained on NASA CALIPSO lidar data, and gives the formulation, the priors and the known weaknesses. [21]

The problem

Most satellite products need to know which pixels are free of cloud. The document names sea-surface temperature and vegetation index as clear-sky applications that depend on the mask. Clouds have no single signature: the mask combines spectral and spatial tests built from brightness temperatures, reflectances and their local variability, and the contrast between clear and cloudy scenes differs over ocean, land, desert, snow and ice. Downstream users also differ in how much risk of contamination they accept, so a bare yes or no is not enough.

Where this topic fits

The mask runs per pixel, before the products that depend on it. Offline, imager pixels collocated with CALIPSO lidar observations, which detect cloud layers directly, serve as labelled training data. From them the distribution of each test's value is tabulated for cloudy and for clear pixels, separately for each surface type. Online, each pixel's test values are looked up in those tables and combined with a prior cloud probability for that place and month.

How it is applied, step by step

  1. Label training pixels with the lidar. A pixel whose collocated CALIPSO column contains at least one cloud layer counts as cloudy, and otherwise as clear.
  2. For each test and surface type, divide the test's value range into bins and record what fraction of all cloudy training pixels, and of all clear ones, falls in each bin. These fractions are the class-conditional likelihoods, and no bell curve is assumed.
  3. Store the ratio of the clear fraction to the cloudy fraction for each bin in a lookup table.
  4. For a new pixel, look up the ratio for each of its test values and multiply the ratios together to get R. The multiplication is the naive Bayes step: it treats the tests as independent given the class.
  5. Combine R with the prior cloud probability for that location and month, taken from a lidar cloud climatology, into the posterior cloud probability 1 / (1 + R / prior - R).
  6. Convert the probability into the four-level mask (confidently clear, probably clear, probably cloudy, confidently cloudy) with thresholds, and publish the probability as well.

Why this approach fits

Each test is a continuous quantity whose distribution differs between clear and cloudy scenes. Estimating a separate distribution for each test, or small group of tests, from collocated data is easy, while the joint distribution of all the tests across seven surface types is not. Binned ratios in a lookup table make the per-pixel cost a few table reads and multiplications, which matters when every pixel of every image is processed. The output is a probability, so users with different tolerances can apply their own thresholds. The prior does real work here: cloud cover varies strongly by region and season, and Bayes' theorem gives that knowledge a principled place in the calculation.

Limitation or tradeoff

The tests are built from the same few spectral channels, so they are correlated, and the document says so: combining classifiers risks reduced performance because of correlations between them. Its mitigations are to add classifiers one at a time, keeping only those that still improve the result, and to let a single classifier be a two- or three-dimensional table of related metrics, which models those metrics jointly. Binned likelihoods are only as good as the training coverage, and conditions that are rare in the collocated data give noisy ratios. The document's own plan is to replace the naive Bayesian method with neural networks and other machine learning approaches, which it reports to be superior for this application.

What the sources document

  • The document describes the ECM as an evolution of the naive Bayesian cloud mask developed for AVHRR PATMOS-x data (Heidinger et al., 2012), still a naive Bayesian approach trained on NASA CALIPSO data, that produces a cloud probability and a four-level cloud mask. [21]
  • Section 7.3 defines class-conditional yes and no values as the fraction of all yes (or no) cases within a bin compared with the total in all bins, multiplies their ratios into R, and gives the posterior as 1 / (1 + R/Pr - R) where Pr is the prior probability; the lookup tables store only the ratio. [21]
  • The prior is derived from a CALIPSO Level 3 monthly cloud product: monthly data from 2007 to 2015 were used to compute mean cloud fractions for each month on a 1 degree by 1 degree grid over the globe. [21]
  • The globe is classified into seven surface types (deep ocean, shallow water, land, snow, Arctic, Antarctic and desert), and the cloud probability threshold between probably cloudy and confidently cloudy is kept at 0.9. [21]
  • The document states that combining classifiers risks reduced performance from correlations between them, describes a sequential optimisation for choosing classifiers, and lists a planned switch from the naive Bayesian method to neural-network and other approaches. [21]

The facts above come from the cited sources. The steps and analysis in this example are our explanation of how they fit together.

Example 5 of 5

GnuCash: suggesting the account for an imported bank transaction

GnuCashDocumented in an open-source project

GnuCash is free double-entry accounting software. When bank transactions are imported, its import matcher proposes the account each one should be booked to. The GnuCash manual calls the mechanism the Bayesian matcher, and the engine source file Account.cpp contains the implementation. [22][23]

The problem

An imported bank statement lists dates, amounts and free-text descriptions, but double-entry bookkeeping needs a second account for every line: groceries, fuel, rent. Assigning these by hand for every import is tedious, and the right mapping is personal, because each user has a different chart of accounts and different payees. The manual says the original matcher recorded only that a token had occurred with an account, not how often.

Where this topic fits

The classifier runs inside the import dialog. The classes are the user's own accounts, the features are tokens from the imported transaction's text, and the training data is the user's earlier imports into the same source account. Each time the user accepts or corrects an assignment and completes the import, the counts are updated, so the model is trained continuously by ordinary use.

How it is applied, step by step

  1. When an import is completed, take the tokens produced from each imported transaction and add one to the count stored for each pair of token and chosen account. Counts are kept separately for each source account.
  2. For a newly imported transaction, produce tokens in the same way.
  3. For each token and each account that has been seen with it, compute the share of the token's occurrences that went to that account: the count for the account divided by the token's total count.
  4. For each candidate account, multiply these shares across the tokens, and separately multiply their complements (one minus each share).
  5. The account's probability is the first product divided by the sum of the two products. This is the two-outcome naive Bayes combination with equal priors, the same formula as in the spam example.
  6. Take the account with the highest probability. If that probability is below 90 %, propose nothing and leave the transaction for the user to assign.

Why this approach fits

Every user starts with no data and builds up a few hundred labelled transactions, too few for a model with many parameters and plenty for counts. The vocabulary is small and repetitive because the same merchants recur, so a shop name quickly becomes strong evidence. Training has to happen invisibly, as a side effect of confirming imports, and a table of counts can be updated in place and saved with the accounts. The 90 % threshold turns the classifier into a suggestion engine that stays silent when it is unsure, which suits a task where a wrong booking costs more than an empty field.

Limitation or tradeoff

As we read the published code, it applies no smoothing and no class prior. A token that has been seen only once, with a single account, gives that account a share of exactly 1, and that forces the account's combined probability to 1 whatever the other tokens say. An account is also scored only on the tokens it has been seen with, so it is not penalised for the ones it lacks. Early in use, one unusual transaction can therefore produce a confident wrong suggestion until more history builds up. The manual provides an Import Map Editor in which users can inspect and delete stored token associations, which is the manual repair for stale or wrong counts.

What the sources document

  • The manual says the import matcher attempts to assign a transfer account from tokenised information stored for previously imported transactions, assigns it when a good match is obtained, and otherwise flags the transaction for manual assignment by the user. [22]
  • The manual describes the Bayesian matcher as using the frequency of association of a token string with an assigned transfer account for a specific source account, and says it superseded an original non-Bayesian matcher that does not record the frequency of association. [22]
  • The manual states that tokenised data from the transactions assigned to a transfer account is stored on exiting the matcher and used in future imports, and that the Import Map Editor allows this data to be edited. [22]
  • In Account.cpp a token's probability for an account is its stored count for that account divided by the token's total count, and a comment gives the combining rule as p(AB) = (a*b)/[a*b + (1-a)(1-b)], implemented as a running product and a running product of the complements. [23]
  • The same file defines a threshold of 90 %, and the function gnc_account_imap_find_account_bayes returns no account when the best probability is below it. [23]

The facts above come from the cited sources. The steps and analysis in this example are our explanation of how they fit together.

4Common mistakes

  1. Switching smoothing off, or never tuning alpha away from whatever value it started with.

    Why it causes problems
    With alpha at 0, a word that was never seen with a class sets that class's probability to zero, so one unusual word overrides all the other evidence, and when every class has such a word the model returns nan. With alpha too large the likelihoods flatten and predictions slide towards the majority class.
    How to recognise it
    Probabilities of exactly 0 or 1, nan outputs or divide-by-zero warnings from scikit-learn. At the other extreme, almost every test row is predicted as the largest class. In exercise 1, raising alpha to 10 flips "package delivery update" from shipping to billing.
    How to fix it
    Keep alpha above 0 and include it in cross-validation, for example over 0.01, 0.1, 0.5 and 1. Choose the value with the best held-out score, not the best training score.

  2. Treating predict_proba as a calibrated probability and setting a business threshold on it.

    Why it causes problems
    Correlated features are counted repeatedly, so scores pile up near 0 and 1. A rule such as "block when P(spam) is above 0.9" then behaves almost like a rule at 0.5, and any expected-cost calculation that multiplies by the probability is wrong.
    How to recognise it
    A histogram of predicted probabilities with nearly everything in the two end bins, a reliability curve far from the diagonal, or held-out predictions of 0.99 that are right clearly less than 99 % of the time.
    How to fix it
    Use only the ranking of the classes, or wrap the model in CalibratedClassifierCV and pick the threshold on held-out data from the precision and recall you need.

  3. Multiplying raw probabilities in a hand-written implementation.

    Why it causes problems
    The product underflows to 0.0 for documents of a few hundred words. Every class then scores zero and the arg max returns whichever class comes first, so long documents are classified arbitrarily.
    How to recognise it
    Long documents all receive the same label while short ones are classified sensibly, and printed scores show 0.0 for every class. With likelihoods around 0.05 the product reaches zero after about 250 words.
    How to fix it
    Add log probabilities. To turn log scores into probabilities, subtract the largest score from each, exponentiate and normalise.

  4. Picking the variant by habit and not by the type of the features.

    Why it causes problems
    GaussianNB on word counts fits a bell curve to columns that are almost entirely zeros. MultinomialNB on standardised features fails with "Negative values in data passed to MultinomialNB". BernoulliNB quietly turns every count into present or absent, discarding how often a word occurred.
    How to recognise it
    An error about negative values or about sparse data being passed where dense data is required, a scaler placed in front of MultinomialNB, or accuracy that changes sharply when you swap one variant for another on the same features.
    How to fix it
    Use multinomial (or complement, for imbalanced classes) for counts, Bernoulli for binary features and Gaussian for continuous ones. For a mix of types, bin the continuous columns and use CategoricalNB, or use a different model.

  5. Fitting the vectoriser on all the data before splitting into training and test sets.

    Why it causes problems
    The vocabulary, and with tf-idf the document frequencies, then include the test documents, so the test never contains an unknown word and the reported accuracy is optimistic. The effect is small with raw counts and larger with tf-idf, min_df or feature selection.
    How to recognise it
    fit_transform on the vectoriser appears before train_test_split or outside the cross-validation loop, and the score drops when the same steps are moved inside a pipeline.
    How to fix it
    Put the vectoriser and the classifier in one Pipeline and cross-validate the pipeline, so the vocabulary is rebuilt from the training part of every fold.

  6. Letting the training mix set the prior when production has a different class mix.

    Why it causes problems
    The prior is the share of each class in the training set. A filter trained on a balanced sample of spam and ham but deployed where 5 % of mail is spam starts every message at even odds and flags too much legitimate mail.
    How to recognise it
    The share of each predicted class in production differs steadily from the share later confirmed, and the errors are mostly false positives for the class that was over-represented in training.
    How to fix it
    Pass the production rates through class_prior (MultinomialNB, BernoulliNB) or priors (GaussianNB), or sample the training set to match them, and re-estimate the rates as they drift.

5Practice

Exercise 1

Build a multinomial naive Bayes ticket router from scratch

CodingBeginnerAbout 50 min (estimate)Hypothetical scenario

A support team wants incoming tickets routed to one of three queues. Nine past tickets have been labelled. The data is invented for practice.

#TicketQueue
1refund for double chargebilling
2invoice shows wrong chargebilling
3update card for invoicebilling
4refund not receivedbilling
5app crash on logintechnical
6login error after updatetechnical
7app shows error screentechnical
8package not receivedshipping
9track my package deliveryshipping

Use only the Python standard library, which is free and runs wherever Python 3 does.

  1. Write train(rows, alpha). It returns the log prior of each queue, the smoothed log likelihood of every vocabulary word in every queue, and the vocabulary. Split tickets on spaces.
  2. Write predict(text, model). It skips words outside the vocabulary, adds logs, and returns the winning queue with the posterior probability of every queue.
  3. With alpha = 1, classify: "refund for wrong invoice", "error on login screen", "package delivery update", "charge not received", "where is my parcel" and "hello there".
  4. For "charge not received", report P(billing) and P(shipping) with alpha = 0.1, 1 and 10, and explain the trend.
  5. Explain the predictions for "where is my parcel" and "hello there" in terms of the prior.

Optional check: if you have scikit-learn, confirm the alpha = 1 posteriors with CountVectorizer and MultinomialNB.

Requirements

  • Estimate each prior as the share of training tickets that belong to the queue.
  • Use the smoothed estimate (count + alpha) / (total words in the class + alpha × vocabulary size), with one vocabulary built from all three classes.
  • Work in log space and convert to probabilities only at the end, subtracting the largest score before exponentiating.
  • Ignore words that are not in the vocabulary, and do not add them to it at prediction time.
  • Report posteriors to three decimals so that they can be compared with the expected values.

Expected behaviour

The vocabulary has 22 words, and billing, technical and shipping contain 15, 12 and 7 word occurrences. With alpha = 1:

  • "refund for wrong invoice" goes to billing with probability 0.958.
  • "error on login screen" goes to technical with 0.942.
  • "package delivery update" goes to shipping with 0.613.
  • "charge not received" goes to billing with 0.701 (shipping 0.243, technical 0.056).
  • "where is my parcel" goes to shipping with 0.413, on one known word.
  • "hello there" returns exactly the priors: billing 0.444, technical 0.333, shipping 0.222.

For "charge not received", P(billing) is 0.865, 0.701 and 0.500 at alpha = 0.1, 1 and 10, and P(shipping) is 0.135, 0.243 and 0.231.

Hint 1

A collections.Counter per class holds the word counts, and the vocabulary is the union of the keys of all three counters.

Hint 2

The denominator for a class is its total number of word occurrences plus alpha times the vocabulary size (22). It is not the number of tickets.

Hint 3

To turn log scores into probabilities, subtract the maximum score from each, exponentiate, and divide by the sum. This avoids underflow.

Show solution
python
import math
from collections import Counter, defaultdict

TRAIN = [
    ("refund for double charge", "billing"),
    ("invoice shows wrong charge", "billing"),
    ("update card for invoice", "billing"),
    ("refund not received", "billing"),
    ("app crash on login", "technical"),
    ("login error after update", "technical"),
    ("app shows error screen", "technical"),
    ("package not received", "shipping"),
    ("track my package delivery", "shipping"),
]
TESTS = [
    "refund for wrong invoice",
    "error on login screen",
    "package delivery update",
    "charge not received",
    "where is my parcel",
    "hello there",
]


def train(rows, alpha=1.0):
    """Count once, then turn the counts into log priors and smoothed log likelihoods."""
    docs_per_class = Counter(label for _, label in rows)
    word_counts = defaultdict(Counter)
    for text, label in rows:
        word_counts[label].update(text.split())
    vocab = sorted({word for counts in word_counts.values() for word in counts})
    log_prior = {c: math.log(n / len(rows)) for c, n in docs_per_class.items()}
    log_like = {}
    for c in docs_per_class:
        total = sum(word_counts[c].values())
        log_like[c] = {
            w: math.log((word_counts[c][w] + alpha) / (total + alpha * len(vocab)))
            for w in vocab
        }
    return log_prior, log_like, set(vocab)


def predict(text, model):
    log_prior, log_like, vocab = model
    known = [w for w in text.split() if w in vocab]      # unseen words are skipped
    scores = {c: log_prior[c] + sum(log_like[c][w] for w in known) for c in log_prior}
    top = max(scores.values())
    norm = top + math.log(sum(math.exp(s - top) for s in scores.values()))   # log-sum-exp
    posterior = {c: math.exp(s - norm) for c, s in scores.items()}
    return max(scores, key=scores.get), posterior, known


model = train(TRAIN, alpha=1.0)
print("vocabulary size:", len(model[2]))
for text in TESTS:
    label, posterior, known = predict(text, model)
    shown = ", ".join(f"{c} {p:.3f}" for c, p in sorted(posterior.items()))
    print(f"{text!r} -> {label}  ({shown})  known words: {len(known)}")

for alpha in (0.1, 1.0, 10.0):
    _, posterior, _ = predict("charge not received", train(TRAIN, alpha))
    print(f"alpha = {alpha}: P(billing) = {posterior['billing']:.3f}, P(shipping) = {posterior['shipping']:.3f}")
text
vocabulary size: 22
'refund for wrong invoice' -> billing  (billing 0.958, shipping 0.024, technical 0.019)  known words: 4
'error on login screen' -> technical  (billing 0.025, shipping 0.033, technical 0.942)  known words: 4
'package delivery update' -> shipping  (billing 0.197, shipping 0.613, technical 0.190)  known words: 3
'charge not received' -> billing  (billing 0.701, shipping 0.243, technical 0.056)  known words: 3
'where is my parcel' -> shipping  (billing 0.323, shipping 0.413, technical 0.264)  known words: 1
'hello there' -> billing  (billing 0.444, shipping 0.222, technical 0.333)  known words: 0
alpha = 0.1: P(billing) = 0.865, P(shipping) = 0.135
alpha = 1.0: P(billing) = 0.701, P(shipping) = 0.243
alpha = 10.0: P(billing) = 0.500, P(shipping) = 0.231

MultinomialNB(alpha=1.0) on CountVectorizer counts gives the same posteriors (checked with scikit-learn 1.9.1).

A hand check for part 3. For "charge not received" with alpha = 1 the denominators are 15+22=3715 + 22 = 3715+22=37 for billing, 7+22=297 + 22 = 297+22=29 for shipping and 12+22=3412 + 22 = 3412+22=34 for technical:

billing: 49×337×237×237=0.0001053shipping: 29×129×229×229=0.0000364technical: 39×134×134×134=0.0000085\begin{aligned} \text{billing: } & \tfrac{4}{9} \times \tfrac{3}{37} \times \tfrac{2}{37} \times \tfrac{2}{37} = 0.0001053 \\ \text{shipping: } & \tfrac{2}{9} \times \tfrac{1}{29} \times \tfrac{2}{29} \times \tfrac{2}{29} = 0.0000364 \\ \text{technical: } & \tfrac{3}{9} \times \tfrac{1}{34} \times \tfrac{1}{34} \times \tfrac{1}{34} = 0.0000085 \end{aligned}billing: shipping: technical: ​94​×373​×372​×372​=0.000105392​×291​×292​×292​=0.000036493​×341​×341​×341​=0.0000085​

The three sum to 0.0001502, and 0.0001053/0.0001502=0.7010.0001053 / 0.0001502 = 0.7010.0001053/0.0001502=0.701.

Part 4. "charge" occurs twice in billing and nowhere else, while "not" and "received" each occur once in billing and once in shipping. With alpha = 0.1 the zero counts for "charge" in the other queues are barely smoothed, so that one word nearly decides the result (0.865). As alpha grows, every likelihood is pulled towards 1/221/221/22, the words matter less, and the posterior drifts towards the priors of 0.444, 0.333 and 0.222. At alpha = 10 it is already 0.500, 0.269 and 0.231, and "package delivery update" has flipped from shipping to billing.

Part 5. In "where is my parcel" only "my" is in the vocabulary. It was seen once, in a shipping ticket, so P(my∣shipping)=2/29P(\text{my} \mid \text{shipping}) = 2/29P(my∣shipping)=2/29 against 1/371/371/37 for billing, and that single weak word just outweighs billing's larger prior: 0.413 to 0.323. The word a person would use, "parcel", is unknown to the model and contributes nothing; nothing in a bag of words says that it means "package". "hello there" has no known words at all, so each score is only the log prior and the output is the class shares of the training set. A real router should send such a ticket to a person or a default queue instead of acting on a 0.444.

Check your answer

  • Is your vocabulary 22 words, with 15, 12 and 7 word occurrences in billing, technical and shipping?
  • Do you get 0.701 for the probability of billing given "charge not received" at alpha = 1?
  • Does "hello there" return exactly the priors 0.444, 0.333 and 0.222?
  • Does the probability of billing for "charge not received" fall from 0.865 to 0.500 as alpha rises from 0.1 to 10?
  • Can you explain why "parcel" contributes nothing to the score while "package" contributes a lot?

Exercise 2

Gaussian naive Bayes by hand, and what a duplicated sensor does to it

AnalysisIntermediateAbout 45 min (estimate)Hypothetical scenario

A maintenance team has labelled ten bearings as healthy or worn after inspection. For each one they recorded a vibration reading and a housing temperature. The data is invented for practice.

BearingVibration (mm/s)Temperature (°C)State
11.641healthy
21.944healthy
32.040healthy
42.245healthy
52.345healthy
62.447worn
72.852worn
83.049worn
93.355worn
103.552worn

A new bearing reads 2.5 mm/s and 46 °C. A calculator or spreadsheet is enough. Python with scikit-learn, which is free, is optional for checking.

  1. For each class, compute the mean and the population variance (divide by 5, as GaussianNB does) of both features.
  2. Compute the normal density of the new reading for each feature and class, and from them P(worn) with equal priors. Which class is predicted?
  3. A second vibration sensor is fitted beside the first and reports identical values. Add it as a third feature and recompute P(worn). Repeat with two extra copies.
  4. Explain why the answer changed although no information was added, and what you would do about it.
  5. Suppose 90 % of bearings in service are healthy. Recompute P(worn) for the two-feature model with priors of 0.9 and 0.1.

Requirements

  • Use the population variance of each feature within each class.
  • Show the four densities for the new reading before combining them.
  • State the predicted class for the two-feature model and for each model with duplicated columns.
  • Explain the change by naming the assumption that the duplicated sensor violates.
  • Give at least one practical remedy for redundant features.

Expected behaviour

  • Means are 2.0 mm/s and 43 °C for healthy, and 3.0 mm/s and 51 °C for worn.
  • Variances are 0.06 and 4.4 for healthy, and 0.148 and 7.6 for worn.
  • Densities at the new reading: vibration 0.203 (healthy) and 0.446 (worn); temperature 0.068 (healthy) and 0.028 (worn).
  • Two features: P(worn) = 0.473, so the prediction is healthy.
  • Vibration counted twice: P(worn) = 0.664, so the prediction becomes worn. Counted three times: 0.813.
  • With priors of 0.9 and 0.1 on the two-feature model: P(worn) = 0.091.
Hint 1

The normal density is exp(−(x − mean)² / (2 × variance)) / sqrt(2π × variance). You can work with variances directly and never take a standard deviation.

Hint 2

A duplicated column has the same mean, variance and reading as the original, so its density is the same number. Adding it multiplies each class score by that density once more.

Hint 3

For part 5, multiply each class's product of densities by its prior before normalising.

Show solution

Part 1. Healthy: vibration mean 10.0/5=2.010.0 / 5 = 2.010.0/5=2.0 and variance (0.16+0.01+0+0.04+0.09)/5=0.06(0.16 + 0.01 + 0 + 0.04 + 0.09) / 5 = 0.06(0.16+0.01+0+0.04+0.09)/5=0.06; temperature mean 43 and variance (4+1+9+4+4)/5=4.4(4 + 1 + 9 + 4 + 4) / 5 = 4.4(4+1+9+4+4)/5=4.4. Worn: vibration mean 3.0 and variance (0.36+0.04+0+0.09+0.25)/5=0.148(0.36 + 0.04 + 0 + 0.09 + 0.25) / 5 = 0.148(0.36+0.04+0+0.09+0.25)/5=0.148; temperature mean 51 and variance (16+1+4+16+1)/5=7.6(16 + 1 + 4 + 16 + 1) / 5 = 7.6(16+1+4+16+1)/5=7.6.

Part 2. Densities of the new reading (2.5 mm/s, 46 °C):

FeatureClassExponent (x−μ)2/2σ2(x-\mu)^2 / 2\sigma^2(x−μ)2/2σ2Density
Vibrationhealthy0.25/0.12=2.0830.25 / 0.12 = 2.0830.25/0.12=2.083e−2.083/2π×0.06=0.203e^{-2.083} / \sqrt{2\pi \times 0.06} = 0.203e−2.083/2π×0.06​=0.203
Vibrationworn0.25/0.296=0.8450.25 / 0.296 = 0.8450.25/0.296=0.845e−0.845/2π×0.148=0.446e^{-0.845} / \sqrt{2\pi \times 0.148} = 0.446e−0.845/2π×0.148​=0.446
Temperaturehealthy9/8.8=1.0239 / 8.8 = 1.0239/8.8=1.023e−1.023/2π×4.4=0.068e^{-1.023} / \sqrt{2\pi \times 4.4} = 0.068e−1.023/2π×4.4​=0.068
Temperatureworn25/15.2=1.64525 / 15.2 = 1.64525/15.2=1.645e−1.645/2π×7.6=0.028e^{-1.645} / \sqrt{2\pi \times 7.6} = 0.028e−1.645/2π×7.6​=0.028

Equal priors cancel, so the scores are the products of the densities, using unrounded values: healthy 0.2028×0.0684=0.013870.2028 \times 0.0684 = 0.013870.2028×0.0684=0.01387 and worn 0.4456×0.0279=0.012450.4456 \times 0.0279 = 0.012450.4456×0.0279=0.01245. P(worn)=0.01245/(0.01387+0.01245)=0.473P(\text{worn}) = 0.01245 / (0.01387 + 0.01245) = 0.473P(worn)=0.01245/(0.01387+0.01245)=0.473. The prediction is healthy, narrowly.

Part 3. The copy has the same densities as the original vibration column, so each score is multiplied by its vibration density again:

ModelHealthy scoreWorn scoreP(worn)Prediction
Vibration + temperature0.013870.012450.473healthy
Vibration twice + temperature0.0028130.0055480.664worn
Vibration three times + temperature0.0005700.0024720.813worn

Part 4. The vibration reading favours worn by a factor of 0.4456/0.2028=2.200.4456 / 0.2028 = 2.200.4456/0.2028=2.20, and the temperature favours healthy by 0.0684/0.0279=2.450.0684 / 0.0279 = 2.450.0684/0.0279=2.45. With one copy of each, temperature wins narrowly. Every extra copy of vibration multiplies the odds of worn by 2.20 again, so one copy is enough to reverse the decision. The model does this because of the conditional independence assumption: it treats each feature as fresh evidence given the class, and a second sensor that repeats the first is the same evidence counted twice. The measurement did not get more reliable; the model was only told so. Remedies: keep one of each group of near-duplicate features (check the correlation between features within each class), or average them into one feature. If redundant features must stay, use a model that can share weight between them, such as logistic regression, and do not read the naive Bayes probability as confidence.

Part 5. Healthy 0.9×0.01387=0.012480.9 \times 0.01387 = 0.012480.9×0.01387=0.01248, worn 0.1×0.01245=0.0012450.1 \times 0.01245 = 0.0012450.1×0.01245=0.001245, and P(worn)=0.001245/0.01373=0.091P(\text{worn}) = 0.001245 / 0.01373 = 0.091P(worn)=0.001245/0.01373=0.091. The likelihoods have not changed; the prior alone moves the answer from 0.473 to 0.091. Which prior is right depends on where the model is used: the inspected sample was half worn, the fleet is not.

Check in code:

python
import numpy as np
from sklearn.naive_bayes import GaussianNB

# columns: vibration (mm/s), temperature (deg C)
healthy = np.array([[1.6, 41], [1.9, 44], [2.0, 40], [2.2, 45], [2.3, 45]])
worn = np.array([[2.4, 47], [2.8, 52], [3.0, 49], [3.3, 55], [3.5, 52]])
X = np.vstack([healthy, worn])
y = np.array(["healthy"] * 5 + ["worn"] * 5)
new = np.array([[2.5, 46.0]])


def p_worn(model, row):
    return float(model.predict_proba(row)[0, list(model.classes_).index("worn")])


model = GaussianNB().fit(X, y)
print("means:", model.theta_.tolist())
print("variances:", np.round(model.var_, 3).tolist())
print(f"two features:          P(worn) = {p_worn(model, new):.3f} -> {model.predict(new)[0]}")

for copies in (1, 2):
    extra = [X[:, [0]]] * copies                      # the same vibration column again
    Xd = np.hstack([X] + extra)
    new_d = np.hstack([new] + [new[:, [0]]] * copies)
    dup = GaussianNB().fit(Xd, y)
    print(f"vibration counted {copies + 1}x: P(worn) = {p_worn(dup, new_d):.3f} -> {dup.predict(new_d)[0]}")

skewed = GaussianNB(priors=[0.9, 0.1]).fit(X, y)       # order follows model.classes_: healthy, worn
print(f"priors 0.9 / 0.1:      P(worn) = {p_worn(skewed, new):.3f} -> {skewed.predict(new)[0]}")

Output with scikit-learn 1.9.1:

text
means: [[2.0, 43.0], [3.0, 51.0]]
variances: [[0.06, 4.4], [0.148, 7.6]]
two features:          P(worn) = 0.473 -> healthy
vibration counted 2x: P(worn) = 0.664 -> worn
vibration counted 3x: P(worn) = 0.813 -> worn
priors 0.9 / 0.1:      P(worn) = 0.091 -> healthy

Check your answer

  • Are your variances 0.06 and 4.4 for healthy and 0.148 and 7.6 for worn? Values of 0.075 and 5.5 mean you divided by 4, not 5.
  • Is the probability of worn 0.473 with two features, 0.664 with vibration counted twice and 0.813 with it counted three times?
  • Did the predicted class change from healthy to worn when the duplicate column was added?
  • Is the probability of worn about 0.091 with priors of 0.9 and 0.1?
  • Can you state in one sentence which assumption the duplicated sensor violates?

6Curated resources

Chosen for accuracy and usefulness, not search rank. Time figures are estimates.

  • 1.9. Naive Bayes — scikit-learn 1.9.1 documentation (opens in a new tab)

    scikit-learn developers

    DocumentationIntermediateFreeAbout 30 minutes (estimate)

    What it teaches
    The reference description of all five scikit-learn variants (Gaussian, multinomial, complement, Bernoulli and categorical) with the exact estimation formula for each, the smoothing parameters, and incremental training with partial_fit for data that does not fit in memory.
    When to use it
    When you move from this lesson to real code and need to know exactly what each class computes, or which variant to try for your feature type.

  • Naive Bayes text classification (Introduction to Information Retrieval, chapter 13) (opens in a new tab)

    Cambridge University Press (online edition hosted by the Stanford NLP Group)

    BookIntermediateFreeAbout 45 minutes (estimate)

    What it teaches
    The multinomial model for text from first principles: the MAP decision rule, why logs are used, the sparseness problem and add-one smoothing, a four-document worked example, and the training and classification algorithms with their running time.
    When to use it
    After the worked example here, when you want a second derivation and the pseudocode. Continue to the following sections of the same chapter for the Bernoulli model and the properties of naive Bayes.

  • Naive Bayes, Text Classification, and Sentiment (Speech and Language Processing, 3rd edition draft, Appendix B) (opens in a new tab)

    Daniel Jurafsky and James H. Martin (Stanford University)

    BookBeginnerFreeAbout 1 hour (estimate)

    What it teaches
    Naive Bayes for sentiment analysis in a patient textbook style: the bag-of-words and independence assumptions, training with add-one smoothing, handling unknown words and stop words, binary naive Bayes, and how to evaluate a text classifier with precision, recall and cross-validation.
    When to use it
    When you want a slower, fuller treatment with a sentiment example, or when you are about to evaluate your first text classifier and need the evaluation sections.

  • A Plan for Spam (opens in a new tab)

    Paul Graham

    ArticleBeginnerFreeAbout 25 minutes (estimate)

    What it teaches
    How a working spam filter was built from token counts in 2002: the tokenising choices, the bias against false positives, the handling of unseen words, and why per-user training makes the filter harder to evade. It is a first-hand account of engineering decisions and not a textbook derivation.
    When to use it
    When you want to see the practical judgement calls around a naive Bayes system, especially before building a filter where one kind of error costs far more than the other.

  • 1.16. Probability calibration — scikit-learn 1.9.1 documentation (opens in a new tab)

    scikit-learn developers

    DocumentationIntermediateFreeAbout 30 minutes (estimate)

    What it teaches
    Why some classifiers, GaussianNB among them, produce probabilities that are too extreme, how to read a calibration curve, and how CalibratedClassifierCV corrects the output with the sigmoid or isotonic method, including when each method is appropriate.
    When to use it
    Before you put a threshold or a cost on a naive Bayes probability, or when a histogram of your predicted probabilities shows almost everything at 0 and 1.
